To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the administration of vitamin D in critically ill surgical patients is associated with a significant decrease in stress‐induced insulin resistance and a significant decrease in the stress‐induced increase in glycaemia.

vitamin D3 supplementation improves the stress‐induced insulin resistance and hyperglycaemia in surgical critically ill patients and that vitamin D3 may be a useful therapeutic option to prevent insulin resistance and hypergylcaemia in these patients.

1) vitamin D supplementation in critically ill patients with stress‐induced insulin resistance improves insulin sensitivity and reduces stress‐induced glycaemia; 2) the beneficial effect of vitamin D on insulin sensitivity and glycaemia was more pronounced in patients with vitamin D deficiency than in those with vitamin D sufficiency; and 3) vitamin D supplementation had no effect on the inflammatory status of critically ill patients.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the effect of vitamin D supplementation in critically ill patients on the incidence of stress‐induced diabetes and insulin resistance.
the effects of vitamin D on glycaemic indices, insulin resistance, and stress‐induced hormone levels in critically ill non‐diabetic and diabetic patients.
the effects of vitamin D on glucose metabolism in critically ill patients.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
vitamin D supplementation in critically ill patients is not associated with a reduction in the incidence of acute kidney injury.
the evidence for a beneficial effect of vitamin D on insulin resistance and glucose homeostasis in non‐diabetes is weak and inconsistent.

vitamin D has a beneficial effect on glycaemic indices in non‐diabetics and in patients with type 2 diabetes mellitus, and it also has a beneficial effect in the improvement of insulin sensitivity in non‐diabetes patients.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
there are some indications that vitamin D deficiency is associated with insulin resistance in humans.
there is no evidence for a role of vitamin D deficiency as a cause of insulin resistance in critically-ill patients, or in the general population.

vitamin D supplementation in critically ill patients may have the following effects on glucose metabolism: (1) attenuates stress‐induced insulin resistance; (2) attenuates stress induced hyperglycaemia in patients with low vitamin D levels; (3) attenuates stress-induced hyperglycaemia by reducing the insulin clearance rate; and (4) attenuates stress-related hyperglycaemia via an anti-inflammatory mechanism.
The main takeaway from our work is that
vitamin D is an important factor in the development of insulin resistance and type 2 diabetes, and it is likely to be a factor in many other chronic diseases.
, for critically ill patients, vitamin D supplementation can help to prevent hyperglycaemia, which is a common problem in critically ill patients, and can also reduce insulin resistance.
vitamin D deficiency is associated with insulin resistance in patients with T2D.
